item.title: Julia Salazar to hold ‘State Budget 101’ town hall in Bushwick on October 1
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: State Senator Julia Salazar will hold a "State Budget 101" town hall on October 1 from 6 to 8 p.m. at 223 Linden St. in Bushwick.
item.content:encoded:
State Senator Julia Salazar will hold a “State Budget 101” town hall on Thursday, Oct. 1, from 6 to 8 p.m. at 223 Linden St. in Bushwick, where she will explain how New York’s budget is made and answer residents’ questions.

The town hall will cover how to get involved in the budget process, what the budget pays for, from roads and hospitals to raising or lowering income taxes, and the policy it carries beyond spending, including immigration, criminal justice, climate and housing. RSVP at nysenate.gov/StateBudget101.

“Want to know why it’s so complicated to tax the rich? Or why some projects in your community get funded, but others don’t?” Salazar wrote in her invitation. “And, did you know our State Budget does more than provide funding and dictate our state taxes? It also includes immigration protections, tenant protections, criminal justice reforms, and more.”

Questions about the event can go to Salazar’s office at (718) 573-1726 or teamsalazar@nysenate.gov. The invitation is in English and Spanish.

Salazar represents State Senate District 18, which covers North and East Brooklyn and Ridgewood, Queens. First elected in 2018, she has focused on tenant rights, affordable housing and rent regulation.

item.title: Bushwick housing lottery opens two one-bedrooms at 1052 Willoughby Avenue for $2,139 a month
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: Households of one to three people earning $78,960 to $122,160 can apply through NYC Housing Connect until Thursday, Oct. 1.
item.content:encoded:
Two one-bedroom apartments at 1052 Willoughby Avenue in Bushwick are available through an NYC Housing Connect lottery at $2,139 a month, and applications close Thursday, October 1.

The apartments are set aside for households earning 80 percent of the area median income. A one-person household must earn $78,960 to $95,040 a year, a two-person household $78,960 to $108,560 and a three-person household $78,960 to $122,160, according to the listing. Households of one to three people can apply. The listing notes that the minimum income may not apply to applicants with Section 8 vouchers or other rental subsidies.

Applications are submitted online through NYC Housing Connect, the city’s affordable-housing portal, and there are no deposits or application fees, according to the listing.

The apartments have hardwood floors, split-system heating and air conditioning, an intercom entry system and security cameras, and some third-floor units have private patios or balconies, the listing says. One small pet up to 50 pounds is allowed per apartment, with a refundable $300 pet deposit that may be required. Tenants pay for electricity, which covers the electric heat and stove; hot water is included in the rent.

The building has eight apartments, and two are being offered in the lottery. It is expected to receive a property tax exemption through the city’s 485-x incentive program, according to the listing. Applicants’ assets are capped at $135,680, according to the listing.

The J, M and Z trains stop at Myrtle Avenue and nearby stations, the L at DeKalb Avenue, Jefferson Street and Morgan Avenue, and the G at Myrtle-Willoughby Avenues, according to the listing.

Another Brooklyn lottery is open on Housing Connect: 815 Kings Highway, which closes October 13.

Featured image: Image via NYC Housing Connect

item.title: New York City wins $131.5 million settlement from DoorDash for delivery workers
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration announced a $131.5 million settlement against DoorDash for violating New York City's Delivery Worker Laws, directing over $115 million to more than 260,000 underpaid delivery workers.
item.content:encoded:
Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani’s administration announced on September 22 a $131.5 million enforcement settlement against DoorDash over what it described as systematic violations of New York City’s Delivery Worker Laws, an action that will send money to more than 260,000 delivery workers the city says the company underpaid, paid late or never paid at all.

The settlement directs more than $115 million to workers and more than $16 million in civil penalties and costs, according to the Mayor’s Office. The office called it the largest worker settlement in New York City history and the largest settlement involving food delivery workers in the United States. Details are posted at nyc.gov/doordash, and the administration’s full announcement is on the city’s site.

Workers do not need to file a claim or submit evidence to be paid, the Mayor’s Office said. The Department of Consumer and Worker Protection identified everyone owed money by analyzing DoorDash’s own records. In late October, the agency’s settlement administrator will email each worker who experienced an underpayment between April 22, 2022 and June 28, 2026, sent to the last email address the worker used with DoorDash and stating the amount owed. Workers can choose an electronic payment or a check by mail; those who do not choose will be mailed a check to their last-known address. Payments begin this fall.

Compensation is calculated at roughly 200 percent of what a worker was underpaid. A worker owed $1,000 who received nothing will get $3,000, the office said, and a worker paid $1,000 later than the law allows will get $2,000.

The Department of Consumer and Worker Protection said its citywide investigation began after dozens of workers reported that DoorDash had failed to pay them, or paid them late, for work they had already performed. Workers Justice Project helped many of those workers file complaints with the agency, which then expanded the investigation using detailed pay data. The agency found DoorDash failed to pay thousands of workers at all and failed to pay thousands more on time.

The agency also found DoorDash violated the city’s Minimum Pay Rate. Although the company raised hourly pay to meet the rate in December 2023, it excluded several categories of trip time and on-call time when calculating compensable time, according to the office. The Minimum Pay Rate, which the city began enforcing in December 2023, is adjusted annually for inflation and is currently $22.13 per hour, excluding tips.

To build the case, the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection said it obtained terabytes of data from DoorDash, including billions of rows documenting how the company treated delivery workers. Its new Research and Analytics Division analyzed the data to identify more than 152 million individual payment transactions and 110 million working hours tied to the investigation.

“When a worker earns a wage, they deserve to be paid that wage – not tomorrow, not after a lawsuit, but on time and in full,” Mamdani said. “DoorDash underpaid more than 260,000 workers, and today we are getting that money back. No corporation is above the law, and this administration will keep fighting until every worker gets the pay and protections they deserve.”

Beyond the payments, the settlement sets up a worker-driven compliance monitoring program meant to catch violations as they happen. DoorDash must submit detailed data reports to the agency every month for three years. Workers Justice Project and the Workers’ Algorithm Observatory will build software that lets workers capture what DoorDash shows them about their trips and pay and share it directly with the city, and Workers Justice Project will run outreach to workers about the tool and their rights. DoorDash is barred from preventing or penalizing workers for using it. The New York Community Trust will issue grants to both organizations across the three-year monitoring period.

The settlement also requires DoorDash to make software updates so the company cannot offer a New York City worker a delivery unless that worker’s time is being recorded as compensable on-call or trip time, and to comply with the pay rule for “batched” trips, ending what the office called the unlawful practice of paying a lower rate for certain legs of a trip. DoorDash must adopt internal controls, preserve compliance records, and have an internal compliance monitor submit an annual report and sworn statement certifying compliance.

“The size of this settlement shows the damage done to workers by wage theft. But it also shows that enforcement matters,” said Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice Julie Su. “In this administration, if you steal workers’ wages, it’s not enough to just pay what you should have paid in the first place.” Department of Consumer and Worker Protection Commissioner Samuel A.A. Levine said the workers were “showing that opaque algorithms will not have the final word when it comes to how much they are paid for the hard work they do.”

The office tied the settlement to a wider enforcement push, saying the administration has secured more than $104 million in additional tips and $725 million in increased wages for delivery workers since January.

“For too long, DoorDash treated workers as disposable-stealing their wages and deactivating them, leaving families without the income they rely on,” said Ligia Guallpa, executive director of Workers’ Justice Project. “We celebrate this victory, but the fight continues: we will keep organizing for job security, safer working conditions, higher pay and respect.”

Rosendo Tacam, a delivery worker and leader of Los Deliveristas Unidos and member of Workers’ Justice Project, said he filed a complaint after DoorDash deactivated him and did not pay him for his last week of work. “I gave DoorDash everything I had, and then they deactivated me and didn’t pay me for my last week of work. I felt angry and disrespected,” Tacam said. “Today, seeing delivery workers get justice is proof that when we organize, we can make companies respect us as the essential workers we were-and continue to be-for our city.”

Council Member Sandy Nurse, who represents Bushwick, said DoorDash “thought they could shortchange their workers and get away with it. Not on our watch.” Council Member Jennifer Gutiérrez said the complex systems delivery workers navigate “doesn’t always allow these low-wage workers to seek justice for the compensation they deserve from big corporations.”

A hotline for workers with questions or who need to update their email address will open at the end of September. A second round of payments is set for early 2027 for a small group of DoorDash workers, because the company is still correcting elements of its compensable-time calculation logic that caused additional underpayments, an issue that may affect workers using DashLink. Delivery workers who believe their rights are being violated can file a complaint with the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection at nyc.gov/workers.

item.title: Greenpointers opens vendor applications for its December 6 holiday market
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: Greenpointers has opened vendor and performer applications for its free Holiday Market on December 6 at Greenpoint Loft, 67 West St, Brooklyn.
item.content:encoded:
Greenpointers has opened vendor applications for its 2026 Holiday Market, a free shopping event set for Sunday, December 6 at the Greenpoint Loft, and it is looking for makers, food vendors and performers to fill the room.

The market runs from 1 to 7 p.m. at the Greenpoint Loft, 67 West St, 5th Floor, in Brooklyn. Admission is free for visitors.

The vendor categories Greenpointers listed include ceramicists, jewelry designers, illustrators, bakers, vintage curators, clothing and accessories brands, beauty brands, food makers, artists and designers, plus, in the organizer’s words, “wonderfully weird things that don’t fit neatly into a category.” Vendors apply through an online application form. Table fees listed on the form run from $225 for a shared 4-foot table without power to $375 for an 8-foot table near an electrical outlet.

Greenpointers is also seeking DJs, musicians, artists, workshop leaders and performers to run free mini-activities during the day, listing ideas such as a holiday craft station, a portrait booth, carolers, live illustration and kids’ activities. People with a pitch can email markets@greenpointers.com.

Greenpointers, a North Brooklyn news site, has run its markets since 2012.

Featured image: Courtesy of Greenpointers

media:content.media:description: Shoppers and vendors pack the 2022 Greenpointers Holiday Market. Courtesy of Greenpointers

item.title: Mayor Mamdani plants an olive tree at Gracie Mansion with Palestinian families from Gaza
item.dc:creator: Bushwick Daily News Desk
item.description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani planted an olive tree at Gracie Mansion on Wednesday night with Palestinian families from Gaza. "May peace be our future," he wrote.
item.content:encoded:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani planted an olive tree at Gracie Mansion on Wednesday night with Palestinian families from Gaza, whom he hosted for dinner at the mayor’s official residence on the Upper East Side. “Last night I planted an olive tree at Gracie Mansion with Palestinian families from Gaza. May peace be our future,” Mamdani wrote Thursday, sharing a video of the evening.

The guests included Palestinian New Yorkers who have lost family members in Gaza and refugees who had to leave their homes, according to the Mayor’s Office. The gathering was meant to honor their contributions to the city and acknowledge the losses they have endured, the office said.

Mamdani posted the video on the day Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the U.N. General Assembly. In the speech, Netanyahu attacked Mamdani, calling him “the antisemitic mayor of New York.”

A few blocks south of U.N. headquarters, protesters sat in the street at First Avenue and East 39th Street to demand an end to U.S. arms to Israel and the genocide in Gaza, and 104 people were arrested. Jewish Voice for Peace, which organized the sit-in, said 400 people took part.

Three North Brooklyn officials were among those arrested: Council Member Jennifer Gutiérrez, whose district covers parts of Williamsburg, Bushwick and Ridgewood; Council Member Chi Ossé, who represents Bedford-Stuyvesant and Crown Heights; and Assembly Member Emily Gallagher, who represents Greenpoint and Williamsburg. Ossé posted a photo of himself in handcuffs with the caption “Free Palestine. Netanyahu burn in hell.”

Featured image: Image: NYC Mayor's Office video
